title.en: On Standing in Front of a Convenience Store Eating Doritos and Accidentally Thinking About What an Economy Actually Is
title.es: De pie frente a una tienda de conveniencia comiendo Doritos y pensando accidentalmente en qué es realmente una economía

body.en:
So I'm standing in front of a 7-Eleven on Guadalupe Street eating Cool Ranch Doritos out of the bag at like 10:40 p.m. on a Tuesday, which is already — and I'm aware of this even as the corn dust is accumulating on my fingers — already a situation that most of the economics you've been taught would describe as a "consumer making a utility-maximizing choice in a competitive retail environment." Which: fine. Except that what's actually happening is that I'm tired and I'm sad about a paragraph I can't finish, and the fluorescent light is doing that thing where it makes everything look like it's already been photographed for an evidence file, and I wanted something that tasted like something, and Doritos taste like something.1

And the kid behind the counter — I don't know his name, I've been in here probably 200 times and I don't know his name, which is itself a datum that the text I'm about to foist on you would know exactly what to do with — the kid gave me my change and our fingers touched for about a tenth of a second during the transaction, and let me tell you, that tenth of a second is not in any model. It is not in the utility function. It is not in the GDP. That kid is selling his body-time — and the text I want you to read uses exactly that phrase, "body-time," which initially sounds like jargon but is in fact the most compressed and honest description of wage labor I've come across — he's selling body-time under conditions of what the author calls "temporal immediacy," meaning he has to sell today's hours today because he cannot store them, he cannot defer them, he cannot compound them, they are gone at midnight whether or not anyone bought them, like day-old bread except it's his life.2

The text is called Composition and Competitiveness: An Economics of Finitude. I need you to read it, and I need to be honest with you about why.

It is not an easy read. It moves through double-entry bookkeeping, phenomenology, the I Ching, the history of Unix, the Large Hadron Collider, Nikola Tesla's pigeons, Kenyan community currencies, the squatter movement in Geneva, and the electrification of civilization, sometimes in the same chapter, without what you would call "warnings." The author himself says this. He says the text transits through accounting, economics, finance, philosophy, history, and physics without warnings, because the world it describes does not pause at disciplinary boundaries. Which is either an act of extraordinary intellectual courage or a way of saying "good luck," and I think it's both, actually, and I think the author knows it's both, and the fact that he says it straight instead of hedging is one of the reasons I trust this text.

Here is what the text does that I have not seen another text do.

It starts from the premise that the foundational unit of economic reasoning is not the market, not the price, not the rational agent, not the production function. It is the ledger. The double-entry ledger that Luca Pacioli codified in 1494 and that Sumerian scribes were basically doing on clay tablets three thousand years before that. And the text says — and this is the part where I sat up and put the Doritos down — it says that the ledger is not a record of what happened. It is the institutional act through which economic reality becomes binding. The entry in the ledger doesn't describe a promise. It constitutes the promise.3 And then the text walks you through Reinach and Austin and Arendt and Wittgenstein and shows you that these people were all, from completely different directions, describing the same phenomenon: that certain acts — promising, forgiving, authorizing, recording — don't report on a world that already exists. They make the world. The debit and the credit are not descriptions. They are performances. And the balance sheet is not a snapshot. It is a discipline of continuation for a shared going concern.

Do you see what just happened there? We went from a 7-Eleven to a "discipline of continuation for a shared going concern." And the thing I need you to understand is that the 7-Eleven IS a shared going concern. It has a balance sheet. The kid behind the counter has a claim on it — his wages are a liability of the entity. The Frito-Lay corporation that supplied the Doritos has a claim. The landlord has a claim. The city of Austin has a claim — property taxes, sales taxes, health inspections. The whole thing is a web of mutual commitments held together by a ledger that must close every period or the thing dies. And the kid's tenth-of-a-second finger-touch during the change transaction is the point where the phenomenology of exchange — the actual lived experience of one finite human being handing something to another finite human being — meets the accounting architecture that makes the exchange intelligible. And neither can be dissolved into the other. And the tension between them is, according to this text, "the permanent site where economic thought must learn to work."

Now. The text does something else that I have to tell you about because it's going to seem strange and I don't want you to bail on it.

It has passages that read like the I Ching. Not quotes from the I Ching — original passages written in the voice and structure of the I Ching, about the commons, the state, and the market. "A spring emerging from the foot of the mountain. It is not made by decree. It is not summoned by bargain. Those who drink must also protect the source." And then: "One drinks from the spring and muddies it, no blame if he learns restraint. Many draw water, yet one repairs the stones, small recognition. Great merit." And look, I know this is going to make some of you uncomfortable, because we have been trained — and I include myself in this, thoroughly — to treat anything that sounds like wisdom literature as either naïve or decorative or both. But what these passages are doing is something that the analytical prose cannot do. They are establishing a register in which the commons is not a "resource management problem" or a "market failure" or a "public good" but a way of being in the world that precedes all of those categories and that all of those categories fail to hold. The I Ching register is the text's way of saying: there are things the ledger cannot see, and they are not less real for being invisible to the ledger, and the discipline of economic thought includes the discipline of knowing where the ledger stops.4

And then — and this is where the text did something to me that I'm still processing — there's a section about Nikola Tesla. And the author places Tesla in a taxonomy of what he calls "modes of existence" — communer, craftsman, capitalist, financier, worker, artisan, family business — and Tesla turns out to be a communer. Not a capitalist, not an inventor-entrepreneur, not a "disruptive innovator." A communer. Someone whose care was directed toward a future he would not inhabit, whose temporal horizon was intergenerational, who could see the rotating magnetic field whole in a single vision in a park in Budapest, who held over three hundred patents but could not hold a company, whose intellectual capital was in abundance and whose financial capital passed through him like water. And Edison promised him fifty thousand dollars for redesigning his generators and when Tesla finished and asked for the money, Edison said: "Tesla, you don't understand our American humor."5

That exchange — "you don't understand our American humor" — is, according to the text, "the worker's temporal asymmetry in miniature: time committed before knowing whether the commitment will be honored, and the capitalist's power to redefine the terms after the fact." And I read that sentence three times and then I had to go take a walk because it is the most precise description of a particular kind of cruelty that I have ever encountered in an economics text, and it is delivered without anger, without denunciation, in the register of — and the author is explicit about this — an electrician at the shopbench. Diagnostic. Factual. Consequential. The electrician does not denounce the wiring. The electrician tells you where the fault is.

I could keep going. I haven't told you about the two-field model — a flow field F whose characteristic structure is the curl of capital seeking return, and a recognition field R whose characteristic structure is the divergence of care — which is borrowed from electromagnetic field theory and which sounds insane until you realize that it's the only framework I've seen that can simultaneously track why a factory closing destroys a community (negative divergence of R) and why the capital that left is now generating returns somewhere else (the curl of F completing its circuit). I haven't told you about the "ghost agent" — the argument that "the consumer" is a manufactured abstraction with no mode of existence, invented by the marginalists in the 1870s to bear the demand function, and that every act economics calls "consumption" is actually performed by someone who is already something else: a worker spending stored body-time, a communer sharing a feast, an artisan acquiring material. I haven't told you about the conservation law — "nothing leaks, but leak" — which is the most honest four words in the text and possibly in economics. I haven't told you about what happens when the text puts the physicist who found the Higgs boson and the economist who navigated the 2008 crisis side by side and shows you that the difference between physics and economics "is not a difference in kind but a difference in the institutional work each collective has managed to sustain."6

But here is what I really need to say, and it's the reason I'm assigning this.

This text is about finitude. It is about the fact that we die. That the kid behind the counter will die. That I will die. That the 7-Eleven will close someday. That the Doritos will be discontinued or renamed or reformulated. That every going concern eventually stops going. And that the seriousness of economic life — the reason the ledger matters, the reason the balance sheet matters, the reason the promise matters — is grounded in the fact that a mortal creature stakes its word on a future it doesn't control. "The promise has weight because the one who makes it will die, and knows it, and makes the promise anyway — across a future they cannot secure."

And if that sentence doesn't do something to you, then I don't know what to tell you. But I think it will. I think it will because you are also mortal creatures who have staked things on futures you cannot secure — you enrolled in this class, which is a temporal commitment; you are building a life, which is a composition under finitude; you are here, which means you haven't given up on the idea that paying attention to how things actually work might be worth the effort.

Read the text. It's hard and it's uneven and it crosses six disciplines without a seatbelt. The author warns you about this upfront. He says its ambition is focused: "to help its readers see the finite and remarkable world we inhabit — not as a set of problems to be optimized, but as a composition to be stewarded, with honest books, sharper perception of who and what is actually in play, and a seriousness of commitment commensurate with the stakes."

I'm standing in front of a 7-Eleven with cheese dust on my fingers, and for the first time in a long time I feel like someone wrote an economics text that would not be embarrassed to find me here.

—

1 The fact that Doritos "taste like something" is itself a marvel of the market's care network — specifications, flavor chemistry, supply chain logistics, packaging engineering, retail distribution. The text would call this the "second object": the market object generated from the commons object (corn, originally a communer's crop, domesticated over millennia in Mesoamerica) by the denomination of money. The Dorito is simultaneously a food and a financial instrument. I am eating a financial instrument.

2 The text does not use the word "exploitation" here. It uses "temporal immediacy." This is not an evasion. It is a precision. "Exploitation" is a verdict. "Temporal immediacy" is a condition. The condition produces the vulnerability. The verdict follows if you want it to, but the condition is prior and more useful, because it tells you where the wiring is, not whose fault it is.

3 This is where the text does something that I think is genuinely new, or at least new to me. It connects Pacioli's double-entry bookkeeping to Austin's speech-act theory to Arendt's account of promising and forgiving, and the connection is not metaphorical. It is structural. A receivable is a promise bound. A write-off is a forgiveness enacted. The ledger moves through time the same way a political community moves through time: by binding the future and releasing the past. If you think that's a stretch, read the argument. It is not a stretch.

4 I want to be careful here because I can already hear some of you thinking "this is where the author goes soft." It isn't. The I Ching passages are diagnostic instruments. The text later introduces a distinction between the "superior person" (junzi) and the "inferior person" (xiaoren) from the I Ching, and it uses it not as a moral category but as an orientational diagnostic — who reads the configuration accurately and acts in accordance with the time, and who misreads it. This is not wisdom literature. It is a compass.

5 Three hundred patents. Could not hold a company. Died in a hotel room with his pigeons. And every server on the planet runs on alternating current. The text says: "The market honored his inventions and destroyed his life." The books that could have read both of Tesla's temporalities — the deep now of his vision and the calendar extension of his intergenerational care — did not exist. Still don't, mostly.

6 The physicist sealed the laboratory. The economist discovered what came out of a laboratory that was never sealed. Same conservation law — mass-energy in equals mass-energy out, or assets equal liabilities plus equity. Different degrees of closure. And the text argues that the difference is not about the nature of the phenomena but about the institutional work required to achieve and sustain closure. "No leakages is not a property of the system. It is the name of the work." That sentence will be with me for a while.
